Anyone can say a supply is locked. Almost nobody can show it.

Pons Codex Protocol V2 is a registry that answers the question instead of arguing about it. Give it a token and a future date and the balance stays put until that date. Give it a token and no date and the balance goes to the dead address. Either way it files a numbered entry, and the entry is the proof.

How an entry gets its numbers: the contract weighs its own balance before and after the transfer and files the difference, so a token that taxes its own transfers files the figure that landed rather than the figure that was requested. Entries carry the wallet, the token, that measured amount, the open date, the block, and one short line the writer chose.

Where it gets uncomfortable for a writer: the open date only moves further away. There is no path back. A seal can grow, it can change hands, and it can be destroyed early by its owner, but it can never be handed back sooner than promised, because that function was never written.

$CDX is the token attached to the registry. Reading the registry costs nothing, writing to it costs gas, and neither ever pays us. The contract has no owner, no pause, no upgrade, no fee switch and nothing to configure, which also means nothing to rescue if you put the wrong thing in.
